Dataset title: Commodity Flow Survey (CFS)
Organization/publisher: Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), U.S. Department of Transportation, and the U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The Commodity Flow Survey (CFS) is a joint effort by the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), U.S. Department of Transportation, and the U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce and is required by law. The survey, conducted every five years, is the primary source of national and state-level data on domestic freight shipments by American businesses. As a shipper-based survey, the CFS collects information on how U.S. establishments transport raw materials and finished goods; the types of commodities shipped by mode of transportation; the value, weight, origin, and destinations of shipments (including exports). # Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Commodity Flow Survey (CFS)
Organization/publisher: Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), U.S. Department of Transportation, and the U.S. Census Bureau
Description: The Commodity Flow Survey (CFS) is a joint effort by the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), U.S. Department of Transportation, and the U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce and is required by law. The survey, conducted every five years, is the primary source of national and state-level data on domestic freight shipments by American businesses. As a shipper-based survey, the CFS collects information on how U.S. establishments transport raw materials and finished goods; the types of commodities shipped by mode of transportation; the value, weight, origin, and destinations of shipments (including exports). The CFS does not include imports or shipments originating in any U.S. territories. Industry coverage includes: Mining, Manufacturing, Wholesale Trade, Select Retail and Services, and some auxiliary establishments (e.g., warehouses) of in-scope, multi-unit, and retail companies.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Commodity Flow Survey comprehensively, verifying your information and gathering details across multiple perspectives.I have strong material on authority and history. Let me gather more on methodology, data products/access, users, and the most recent survey status.# Comprehensive Research Report: The Commodity Flow Survey (CFS)

## 1. Verification of Your Provided Information

**Your information is accurate.** The description you provided matches the official language on the Census Bureau's CFS "About" page nearly verbatim. Confirmed facts:

- **Publishers:** Joint effort of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), U.S. DOT, and the U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) is also a named partner, particularly for the hazardous materials components.
- **Legal requirement:** Yes, response is mandatory by law (details below).
- **Frequency:** Every five years, in years ending in "2" and "7," as a component of the Economic Census.
- **Scope:** Shipper-based survey of domestic freight shipments; excludes imports and shipments originating in U.S. territories; covers exports (domestic leg and destination country).
- **Industry coverage:** Mining, Manufacturing, Wholesale Trade, select Retail and Services, plus auxiliary establishments (warehouses, distribution centers, managing offices) of in-scope multi-unit companies.

One small refinement: the survey is described as covering "approximately three-fourths of all freight movements" by value/weight of in-scope sectors, and it is the **only publicly available source of commodity flows by highway**, which is the dominant freight mode.

---

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

The CFS rests on a dual statutory foundation:

**Census Bureau authority (Department of Commerce):**
- **Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 8(b), 131, and 193** — authorize the survey as part of the quinquennial Economic Census.
- **Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 224 and 225** — make response **mandatory**; non-response can bring prosecution and fines up to $5,000 (per the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3559, 3571), and response is still required.
- **Title 13 U.S.C. § 9** — guarantees **confidentiality**: responses may be seen only by sworn Census employees, used only for statistical purposes, and copies retained by respondents are immune from legal process. Violations by staff carry penalties up to 5 years imprisonment and $250,000 in fines (13 U.S.C. § 214; 18 U.S.C. §§ 3559, 3571).

**BTS authority (Department of Transportation):**
- **49 U.S.C. § 6302** — BTS's enabling statute, mandating collection of economic data on transportation mode choice and goods movement.
- **49 U.S.C. § 6313** — "Mandatory response authority for freight data collection," added by MAP-21 (Pub. L. 112-141, 2012), authorizing fines for freight entities that refuse BTS data requests (up to $500; up to $10,000 for willfully false answers).

**Administrative authority:** The survey operates under OMB Control Number **0607-0932**, renewed each cycle through the Paperwork Reduction Act process (Federal Register notices, e.g., 86 FR 60614 for 2022; 91 FR 29449 for 2027).

---

## 3. History and Evolution

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| 1963–1977 | Predecessor **Commodity Transportation Survey (CTS)** — limited to manufacturing establishments (~20,000), last published for 1977 |
| 1983 | CTS conducted but data **never published**; no 1987 survey |
| 1980s | Transportation deregulation dramatically reduced freight regulatory data, creating a ~15-year gap in national freight statistics |
| Dec. 18, 1991 | **Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act (ISTEA)** creates BTS, partly to fill the freight data gap |
| 1992 | BTS–Census Bureau partnership formed (Census brought the establishment frame, mandatory authority, and survey infrastructure; BTS historically provided ~80% of funding, Census ~20%) |
| 1993 | **First CFS** (delayed one year past the 1992 Economic Census because BTS didn't exist yet) |
| 1997–2017 | Surveys in 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017; 2004 Research and Innovative Technology Act moves BTS within RITA/OST-R |
| 2017 | First **Public Use File (PUF)** released experimentally; temperature-controlled shipment data introduced; ~104,000 establishments sampled |
| 2022 | **Seventh CFS**: ~165,000 establishments; respondents could report *all* shipments in a week; **noise infusion** adopted for disclosure avoidance; final estimates released **June 2025**, full publication **January 20, 2026**, and **Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) January 28, 2026** |
| 2027 | Eighth survey in planning: Federal Register notice published May 2026 (comments due July 20, 2026); sample reduced to ~140,000; hazmat packaging supplemental questions dropped; machine learning to be used for commodity coding |

---

## 4. Methodology (for Data Scientists)

**Sample design (three-stage, stratified):**
1. **Stage 1 — Establishments:** stratified random sample from the Census Business Register, stratified by geography × industry × measure-of-size class, with certainty selection for the largest shippers (2017: 103,877 establishments, 51,266 certainty; 2022: ~165,000).
2. **Stage 2 — Reporting weeks:** each establishment reports for one assigned week per calendar quarter (four reports per year).
3. **Stage 3 — Shipments:** establishments report a sample of shipments (or, since 2022, optionally all shipments) for the reporting week; poststratification aligns estimates with totals.

**Data collected per shipment:** commodity (coded to the **Standard Classification of Transported Goods, SCTG** — jointly maintained with Statistics Canada), value, weight, origin/destination (U.S. ZIP-based plus export country), mode(s) of transport, whether hazmat (UN/NA code), whether temperature-controlled, and whether an export. Distances and ton-miles are computed via routing algorithms.

**Geography:** U.S., census regions/divisions, states, and ~120+ "CFS Areas" (metropolitan areas plus remainder-of-state areas).

**Disclosure avoidance (2022):** noise infusion, topcoding (shipment values truncated at $30M in the PUMS), confidential collapsing of rare origins/commodities, and data coarsening. This is important for **longitudinal comparability**: the 2022 PUMS differs structurally from the 2017 PUF (sample vs. full file, no QUARTER variable, different mode collapsing).

**Key exclusions/limitations:** no imports, no U.S. territories origins, limited coverage of agriculture, construction, services, retail, government, and household goods; shipper-based (not carrier-based), so it doesn't directly measure carrier operations.

---

## 5. Data Products and Access (for Data Librarians)

| Product | Description | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Geographic Area Series (GAS)** tables | ~21 tables; shipment characteristics by geography, mode, distance, weight, NAICS, SCTG, origin×destination (some tables have millions of rows) | data.census.gov, CSV downloads, Census API |
| **Hazardous Materials Series** | Hazmat shipments by UN/NA class, mode, geography | Same channels; also BTS cfsdata.bts.gov |
| **Exports Series** | Export shipments by commodity, mode, destination country | Same |
| **Temperature Control Series** | Refrigerated/temperature-controlled shipments | Same |
| **Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS)** | Shipment-level microdata (2022: ~37.6M records, 18 variables, ~680 MB CSV), with tabulation weights and guidance for variance estimation | Census FTP/downloads |
| **Census Data API** | Programmatic access to GAS, Temperature, Exports, Hazmat series (API key required) | census.gov/data/developers |
| **BTS CFS tables** | Thematic subsets | cfsdata.bts.gov |
| **Protected microdata (Title 13)** | Full confidential data accessible via approved projects in **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)** | Proposal-based |
| **Freight Analysis Framework (FAF)** | Derivative product: CFS integrated with trade, agricultural, energy, and other data to model *all* freight flows; FAF6 base year 2022; state and regional databases (CSV/Access); experimental county-to-county flows (Jan 2025) | bts.gov/faf |

**Preservation notes:** Historical datasets back to 1993 remain posted on census.gov (with methodology PDFs, questionnaires, SCTG manuals, and user guides archived at www2.census.gov). The series is cataloged on data.gov. Format longevity is good (CSV), but URL migrations across Census redesigns are a known fragility — preservationists should harvest the www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/cfs/ directory tree, methodology documents, and codebooks alongside the data.

---

## 6. Typical Users and Use Cases

- **Federal agencies:** FHWA (FAF, freight planning, performance measures), PHMSA (hazmat routing and safety analysis), USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (publicly endorsed the 2027 survey — agricultural supply chains), FEMA/emergency planners (supply chain disruption), GAO/CRS analysis.
- **State DOTs and Metropolitan Planning Organizations:** freight plans, corridor investment, State Freight Plans required for federal formula funding.
- **Policy analysts:** assessing demand for transportation facilities and services, energy use, safety risk, environmental impact, regional economic development.
- **Private sector:** logistics network design, site selection, market trend analysis, demand forecasting for infrastructure and equipment.
- **Academia/researchers:** freight modeling, spatial analysis of commodity flows, simulation calibration and validation (the PUMS is explicitly promoted for this).
- **Benchmark economic statistics:** CFS feeds into national economic measurement as an Economic Census component.

---

## 7. Public Benefits

1. **Unique and irreplaceable:** It is the *only* comprehensive, publicly available, multimodal, system-wide source on the volume and pattern of U.S. goods movement — and the only public source for highway commodity flows, the dominant mode.
2. **Infrastructure investment:** Directly informs billions of dollars in federal, state, and local transportation investment decisions and federal freight policy (the National Freight Strategic Plan relies on FAF/CFS).
3. **Safety and environment:** Hazmat flow data supports PHMSA rulemaking and emergency-response planning; flow data underpin emissions and energy-use analysis.
4. **Economic resilience:** Enables analysis of supply chain vulnerabilities — acutely relevant post-2020.
5. **Equity of access:** Published estimates, a free API, and microdata products make high-value freight intelligence available to small jurisdictions and researchers, not just firms that can buy proprietary data.

---

## 8. Risks and Considerations for Preservationists and Policy Activists

- **Five-year cadence with long latency:** The 2022 survey's final estimates appeared in mid-2025, publication in early 2026 — a 3+ year lag. Any cancellation (as happened to the CTS in 1983, when data were collected but never published) would leave a 10-year hole.
- **Funding vulnerability:** CFS depends on the BTS–Census partnership and Economic Census appropriations. FY2026–27 Census budget debates show proposed funding hundreds of millions below agency requests, and the Periodic Economic Statistics account (which funds the Economic Census) has faced proposed cuts.
- **Scope reduction in 2027:** The hazmat packaging supplement is being removed and the sample cut ~15% (165k→140k) — relevant for trend analysis and advocacy.
- **Disclosure-avoidance changes:** The 2022 shift to noise infusion means published values are perturbed; researchers must consult methodology documents before pooling cycles. The PUF→PUMS change also altered microdata structure.
- **Coverage gaps as advocacy targets:** Agriculture, construction, services, imports, and territories remain out of scope; the FAF partially compensates by imputation, but activists pushing for better freight data (e.g., near-real-time or more granular geography) should note the experimental county-to-county FAF product as a sign of demand.
- **Confidentiality vs. access tension:** Title 13 protections are strong (a benefit for respondent trust) but mean true microdata requires FSRDC access; the PUMS is heavily coarsened.

---

## Key Sources

- Census Bureau CFS portal: census.gov/programs-surveys/cfs (About, Methodology, Questionnaires, Updates)
- BTS CFS portal and FAQs: bts.gov/cfs; BTS data tables: cfsdata.bts.gov
- 2022 CFS PUMS User's Guide: www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/cfs/datasets/2022/cfs_2022_pums_users_guide.pdf
- Federal Register ICR notices: 86 FR 60614 (2022 CFS); 91 FR 29449 (2027 CFS)
- Statutes: 13 U.S.C. §§ 8(b), 9, 131, 193, 224, 225; 49 U.S.C. §§ 6302, 6313
- TRB Circular E-C088, "Commodity Flow Survey" (history of the CTS→CFS transition): trb.org/publications/circulars/ec088.pdf
- Freight Analysis Framework: bts.gov/faf

If you'd like, I can go deeper on any thread — e.g., the SCTG classification system, FAF methodology, the FSRDC proposal process, or a cycle-by-cycle comparability table for 1993–2022.

Let me verify the 2027 CFS ICR status, historical data availability on census.gov, and any 2025-2026 policy changes specifically affecting the CFS.Let me get specifics on Census Bureau and BTS staffing losses and leadership changes in 2025–2026.# Risk Assessment: Commodity Flow Survey (CFS)

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- CFS historical datasets from **1993 through 2022** remain publicly posted on census.gov, including the historical datasets page (census.gov/data/datasets/2022/econ/cfs/historical-datasets.html), methodology PDFs, questionnaires, the 2017 Public Use File, and the 2022 PUMS on www2.census.gov. BTS mirrors thematic tables at cfsdata.bts.gov. No CFS-specific file removals have been reported or observed.
- *Environmental caveat:* In January–February 2025, the Census Bureau took large portions of its site offline and removed 3,000+ pages (mostly research/methodology and gender-related content) in response to Executive Order 14168; data.census.gov was intermittently inaccessible, and over 3,300 datasets temporarily disappeared from Data.gov government-wide. Court orders and public pressure led to restoration of most content. CFS data files were not identified among removed material, but the episode demonstrates that removal can happen quickly and without notice.

**Selected level: No Known Issue** — All prior-cycle CFS data remain accessible with no known alterations. The January 2025 purge precedent is a systemic concern but produced no documented CFS impact, so it does not meet the Moderate threshold of actual removed elements.

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- The 2022 CFS was fully published: final estimates June 2025, complete publication January 20, 2026, and the PUMS January 28, 2026 (BTS newsroom; Census 2022 CFS releases). The lag (~2.5–3 years post-reference-year) is consistent with historical norms for this survey (2017 CFS took ~3 years amid COVID).
- The 2027 cycle is proceeding on schedule: the Census Bureau published the 60-day Federal Register notice for **reinstatement with change of OMB 0607-0932** on May 20, 2026 (91 FR 29449; Docket USBC-2026-0166), with comments due July 20, 2026 — the normal runway for a 2027 collection year. The 2022 ICR shows "Historical Active" status at reginfo.gov; expiration between quinquennial cycles is routine and the reinstatement is in motion well in advance, so there is no lapse.
- No statutory publication deadline has been missed; no cycle has been skipped. (Precedent exists for failure — the 1983 predecessor CTS was collected but never published — but nothing indicates repetition.)
- *Watch item:* The House FY2027 CJS appropriations bill would fund the Periodic Censuses and Programs account ~30% below the Administration's request, which advocates warn is inadequate for the 2027 Economic Census ramp-up (The Census Project, May 2026). If enacted at that level, delay risk would rise.

**Selected level: No Known Issue** — Publication is current, and the ICR renewal is active and on track with no lapse. Funding risk is real but prospective; it is captured under Staffing and Funding rather than here, since no deadline or cycle has actually been missed.

## Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- 2022 cycle *improved* some dimensions: larger sample (~165,000 establishments, up from ~104,000), option to report all shipments in a week, new PUMS microdata product, and continued temperature-control and hazmat series. Offsetting this, 2022 introduced **noise infusion** disclosure avoidance and a restructured microdata product (PUMS replacing the PUF), reducing precision and longitudinal comparability.
- 2027 proposals (91 FR 29449) would: **reduce the sample ~15%** (165,000 → 140,000 establishments), **eliminate the hazardous materials packaging supplemental questions and their respondents**, and shift commodity coding to machine learning. The notice frames these as burden reduction. A smaller sample typically means more suppressed or noisier cells at detailed geography/commodity/mode crossings — a genuine potential granularity reduction — and the hazmat packaging removal eliminates data elements entirely.
- These changes are proposed, pending OMB approval; frequency (quinquennial) and timeliness are not threatened in the notice.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk** — There are concrete, documented, pending proposals to reduce content (hazmat packaging) and sample size (potential granularity loss), which fits "potential or emerging risk." It does not yet meet High Risk because the reductions are not finalized and core granularity/frequency are maintained; if OMB approves the package as proposed, this should be re-evaluated toward High.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- Explicit statutory authority: **Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 8(b), 131, 193** (Economic Census), and **49 U.S.C. § 6302** (BTS mandate), cited in the ICR itself; mandatory response backed by 13 U.S.C. §§ 224–225 and 49 U.S.C. § 6313 (freight data collection authority added by MAP-21). The CFS is a named component of the statutorily required quinquennial Economic Census.
- **No substitute exists:** the CFS is described in the government's own FR notice as "the only comprehensive and publicly available source of multimodal, system-wide data" on U.S. goods movement, and the only public source for highway commodity flows. FAF is derived *from* CFS, not a substitute.
- Clear programmatic use: federal freight policy and formula-driven state freight planning (FHWA), PHMSA hazmat safety, USDA agricultural supply-chain analysis (USDA's May 1, 2026 letter of "strong support"), and National Freight Strategic Plan.

**Selected level: No Known Issue** — Authorization is explicit and specific, response is mandatory by statute, the survey is embedded in a required census, and no alternative collection could substitute.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- **BTS: ~31% staff loss in FY2025** (from ~75 FTE; American Statistical Association, *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025*, Table 2.1). DOT-wide cuts exceeded 25–30% in several operating administrations (ENO); DOT conducted DRP rounds and RIFs in 2025 (GovExec). BTS has long-standing capacity fragility: it is the smallest principal statistical agency, lost 46% of purchasing power since FY2003, sits four levels below the Secretary, and its Director position is currently **Acting** (Ed Strocko, per the BTS staff directory), with the Deputy Director and Statistical Policy Team Director positions vacant.
- **Census Bureau: ~15% staff loss since FY2024** (ASA); ~1,300+ employees departed via DRP/early retirement (AP; AFGE Council 241). Critically for CFS, the FY2026 request proposed a **27% staffing cut to the Periodic Censuses and Programs account** (1,761 vs. 2,426 FTE in FY24) — the account that houses the Economic Census/CFS.
- **Leadership removed:** Census Director Robert Santos resigned February 2025, mid-fixed-term; the Bureau has been run by acting leadership (Ron Jarmin) with 18 top-leadership vacancies reported (AP). This independently meets the High Risk trigger.
- **Budget:** FY2026 Periodic Economic Statistics request was cut ~$18M vs. FY2024 (CRS IF12714). FY2027 request *increases* Periodic Censuses +47% (driven by 2030 Census), but the House committee bill would cut the account 30% below request. No enacted 20%+ agency budget cut yet.

**Selected level: High Risk** — Multiple rubric triggers are met: more than 1,000 staff lost at Census alone (~1,300), BTS staffing down ~31%, and leadership removal/vacancy at both partner agencies. Note these are agency- and account-level figures, not CFS-program-specific — the CFS team itself is small and embedded in the Economic Census directorate — but the survey depends entirely on these degraded institutions.

## Policy

**Evidence:**
- No termination or negative policy note targeting CFS; the 2027 reinstatement was initiated by the current administration, and an administration agency (USDA AMS) formally endorsed it — a positive signal.
- However, **changes to what is collected are formally proposed and pending** under this administration's ICR: removal of hazmat packaging content, ~15% sample reduction, framed around respondent-burden reduction consistent with administration deregulatory priorities (91 FR 29449).
- Broader environment: EO 14168-driven removals of Census content (gender-identity-related) and temporary data.census.gov outages in early 2025 show willingness to alter data dissemination for policy reasons; DOGE accessed multiple statistical agencies; BLS and NCES heads were removed; other surveys (e.g., CPS Food Security Supplement) were terminated by policy decision. None of these actions touched CFS content directly, and the 2027 ICR does not appear to be a Presidential-Action-driven collection.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk** — There are proposed/pending changes to collection content initiated since January 2025 (the hazmat packaging removal and sample cut), fitting "proposed or pending changes." High Risk is not met because the ICR is a regular reinstatement rather than a Presidential-Action-driven collection, and there is no negative policy note or termination signal specific to CFS — indeed, intra-administration support exists.

## Summary

Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue
Future Data Availability: No Known Issue
Data Quality: Moderate Risk
Statutory Context: No Known Issue
Staffing and Funding: High Risk
Policy: Moderate Risk

**Overall:** The CFS enjoys exceptionally strong statutory and programmatic protection — it is legally required, unique, and actively supported across agencies — and its historical record and 2027 planning remain intact. The dominant risk vector is not policy hostility toward the survey itself but **institutional capacity**: a ~31% staff loss at BTS, ~1,300 departures and acting leadership at Census, and a proposed 27% cut to the very account that will run the 2027 Economic Census. The pending 2027 content reductions (hazmat packaging, smaller sample) are the leading indicator to monitor; preservationists should treat the current window — with all 1993–2022 files, PUMS, and methodology documents still online — as the right time to archive comprehensively, given both the demonstrated speed of January 2025-era website actions and the staffing-driven fragility of the agencies that would restore them.
